P0011.title: Amazon raises clothing and handbag referral fees as FBA fees rise on February 22
P0011.alt: A brass hanging balance scale tips with a stack of coins on one pan and a twine-tied parcel on the other.
P0011.ttag: Amazon raises clothing and handbag referral fees as FBA fees rise on February 22 | Kwontified
P0011.desc: Amazon told sellers on January 18, 2018 that it will raise referral fees for Clothing & Accessories and for Shoes, Handbags & Sunglasses from April 15,…
P0011.byline: By Kwontified. Published Jan 19, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0011.body:
Amazon told sellers on January 18, 2018 that it will raise referral fees for Clothing & Accessories and for Shoes, Handbags & Sunglasses from April 15, and cut them for higher-priced jewelry from February 22, according to the notice sellers posted. The changes add to the Fulfillment by Amazon fee increases announced in December, which also take effect on February 22.

What happened

Clothing costs more to sell. The referral fee for Clothing & Accessories rises from 15% to 17% of the sale price from April 15, with a $1.00 minimum per item, according to the notice; a $20 item will pay $3.40 instead of $3.00. In Shoes, Handbags & Sunglasses, items priced above $75 will pay 18%, while items up to $75 stay at 15%.

Jewelry costs less at the top. From February 22, for one year, eligible jewelry will pay 20% on the first $250 of the price and 5% on the rest, with a $2.00 minimum, down from a flat 20%.

Fulfillment costs rise first. Amazon said in December that new FBA fees take effect on February 22, applied year-round with no separate October-to-December rate, and that it will calculate dimensional weight by dividing a unit’s volume by 139 rather than 166, EcommerceBytes reported on December 19. Storage fee changes are to be announced in early 2018.

Why it matters for brands

Apparel margins are squeezed twice. A clothing brand selling through FBA pays the higher fulfillment fee from February 22 and the higher referral fee from April 15, so the break-even price for each product moves up in two steps this spring.

Light, bulky products feel the dimensional change most. A smaller divisor makes a box’s dimensional weight larger, so products with large packaging relative to their weight can move into a higher fee tier without any change to the product.

Advertising budgets are affected too. When fees rise, the amount a brand can afford to spend on advertising for each sale falls by the same amount, unless prices rise.

What to do now

  1. Recalculate the margin on every Amazon product using the February 22 FBA fees and, for apparel, the April 15 referral fees.
  2. Measure your packaging for products near a size or weight tier and check whether the new dimensional weight moves them up.
  3. Lower the maximum advertising cost per sale for any product whose margin falls, before April 15.

P0035.title: Google launches Shopping Actions, a shared cart for retailers across Search and Assistant
P0035.alt: A gray fabric smart speaker beside a bowl of lemons and a notepad on a sunlit wooden table against a sage wall.
P0035.ttag: Google launches Shopping Actions, a shared cart for retailers across Search and Assistant | Kwontified
P0035.desc: Google launched Shopping Actions on March 19, 2018, a program that lets shoppers buy retailers’ products through Google Search and the Google Assistant…
P0035.byline: By Kwontified. Published Mar 20, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0035.body:
Google launched Shopping Actions on March 19, 2018, a program that lets shoppers buy retailers’ products through Google Search and the Google Assistant with a single cart that works on phones, computers and Google Home speakers, according to Google’s announcement. Retailers including Target, Walmart, Home Depot, Costco and Ulta Beauty are early partners and will pay Google for each purchase made through the program, Reuters reported.

What happened

Shoppers can buy without leaving Google. The program offers a shareable list, a universal shopping cart and instant checkout with saved payment details across Google.com and the Assistant, according to the Reuters report. In the example Reuters described, a shopper searches for hand soap, adds a Target listing to a cart, later adds aluminum foil by voice on a Google Home speaker and buys both in one checkout.

Retailers pay per sale. Rather than paying for clicks, participating retailers will pay Google for each product purchase made through Search, Google Express and the Assistant, Reuters said. The listings appear in the sponsored Shopping unit on Google’s search results and on Google Shopping, and Google said organic rankings will not change, Voicebot reported.

Early results are positive. Target, one of the first retailers to test the program through Google Express, has seen the size of shoppers’ Express baskets increase by nearly 20% over the last six months, and Ulta Beauty’s average order value on Google Express has risen 35% since 2016, according to Google.

Why it matters for brands

Google is building a marketplace of retailers. Shoppers can now buy from several large retailers in one Google cart, which gives those retailers a shared alternative to Amazon’s one-stop store.

A brand’s products may appear through its retailers. Where a brand’s products are sold by participating retailers, they can show up in Google’s shopping results and voice orders under the retailer’s listing, priced and described by the retailer.

Product information travels further. Shopping Actions relies on retailers’ product feeds, so the names, images and prices brands supply to retail partners now also shape how products appear on Google.

What to do now

  1. Ask your largest retail partners whether they are joining Shopping Actions and which of your products they will list.
  2. Review the product names, images and descriptions you supply to those retailers, since they may now appear on Google.
  3. Search Google Shopping for your top products each month to see which retailers’ listings appear and at what prices.

P0038.title: Instagram opens shoppable posts to businesses in eight more countries
P0038.alt: A phone on a small flexible tripod beside white canvas sneakers on a white block against a pink wall.
P0038.ttag: Instagram opens shoppable posts to businesses in eight more countries | Kwontified
P0038.desc: Instagram expanded shopping on Instagram, which lets businesses tag products in their posts, to the UK, France, Italy, Germany, Australia, Brazil, Canada…
P0038.byline: By Kwontified. Published Mar 21, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0038.body:
Instagram expanded shopping on Instagram, which lets businesses tag products in their posts, to the UK, France, Italy, Germany, Australia, Brazil, Canada and Spain on March 20, 2018, Marketing Land reported. The feature had been available only to businesses in the US.

What happened

Businesses outside the US can now tag products. Merchants in the eight new markets can tag up to five products in a single image or up to 20 in a multi-image post, according to Candid, and shoppers get pricing and product details in the feed and through a shop button on the business’s profile, Marketing Land reported.

The audience is large. About half of Instagram’s daily active users in the US follow a shopping business account, and more than 200 million accounts visit at least one business profile daily, according to the company, as reported by Marketing Land. Brazil, one of the new markets, is Instagram’s second-largest market after the US, VentureBeat noted.

There are requirements. To use the feature, a business must sell physical goods, be located in one of the eligible countries, use an Instagram business profile and connect it to a Facebook product catalog, which can be managed through Facebook’s Business Manager or platforms such as Shopify and BigCommerce, according to a guide from Candid.

Why it matters for brands

International brands can now tag products in their home markets. A brand selling in the UK, Europe, Australia, Brazil or Canada no longer needs a US business presence to make its Instagram posts shoppable.

The catalog is the gate. Shoppable posts depend on a connected product catalog, so the quality of a brand’s product data decides whether, and how well, its products can be tagged.

Reach will be competitive. Instagram has said it plans to earn money from shopping by charging businesses to show shoppable posts to people who do not follow them, so the free, organic period in each new market is the cheapest time to learn the tool.

What to do now

  1. If you sell in any of the eight new markets, confirm your Instagram account is a business profile and connected to a Facebook catalog.
  2. Check that the catalog for each market has accurate local prices, descriptions and images.
  3. Tag products in your next posts and track product-detail views and product-page visits.

P0059.crumb: Walmart agrees to buy about 77% of…
P0059.title: Walmart agrees to buy about 77% of Flipkart for $16 billion
P0059.alt: A blue shopping basket of bread, apples, milk, and a bottle on a yellow stool against a bright blue wall.
P0059.ttag: Walmart agrees to buy about 77% of Flipkart for $16 billion | Kwontified
P0059.desc: Walmart said on May 9, 2018 that it has signed agreements to buy a stake of approximately 77% in Flipkart Group, India’s largest e-commerce company, for…
P0059.byline: By Kwontified. Published May 10, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0059.body:
Walmart said on May 9, 2018 that it has signed agreements to buy a stake of approximately 77% in Flipkart Group, India’s largest e-commerce company, for about $16 billion, subject to regulatory approval in India, according to Walmart’s announcement filed with the SEC. The investment includes $2 billion of new equity funding, and the deal values Flipkart at $20.8 billion, TechCrunch reported.

What happened

It is the largest deal Walmart has made. Coverage called it the biggest acquisition in the retailer’s history, Talk Business & Politics reported. Flipkart had gross merchandise value of $7.5 billion in its fiscal year ending March 31, 2018, according to Walmart’s announcement.

Walmart is betting on growth, not current profit. On the call with analysts, chief executive Doug McMillon described India as one of the most attractive retail markets in the world, citing its 1.3 billion people and a growing middle class, and said Walmart expects e-commerce in India to grow at four times the rate of overall retail, according to the call transcript.

The deal is not closed. It still needs regulatory approval in India, and Walmart said its stake could fall somewhat if other investors join the funding round, while it would keep a clear majority.

Why it matters for brands

Walmart’s marketplace ambitions are now global. The company that is building a third-party marketplace in the US has bought a marketplace business abroad that already operates at scale, which tells brands how central marketplaces have become to Walmart’s plans.

Amazon and Walmart will compete in another major market. Both companies now have large bets on Indian e-commerce, so brands that sell in India should expect competition between the two platforms for sellers, selection and shoppers.

The lessons will travel. What Walmart learns from running a large marketplace with outside sellers in India may shape how it runs Walmart.com, where its own marketplace is still growing.

What to do now

  1. If you sell in India, map where your products appear on Flipkart and Amazon India today, and who is selling them.
  2. If you sell on Walmart.com, watch for changes to its marketplace rules and seller programs over the coming year as the two businesses share practices.
  3. Revisit any plan for India that assumed one dominant marketplace; it should now assume two well-funded ones.

P0068.crumb: GDPR takes effect across the EU, with…
P0068.title: GDPR takes effect across the EU, with fines up to 4% of global turnover
P0068.alt: Trestle table with wooden crates, ceramic bowls, folded towels and woven baskets against a sunlit terracotta wall.
P0068.ttag: GDPR takes effect across the EU, with fines up to 4% of global turnover | Kwontified
P0068.desc: The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation takes effect today, May 25, 2018, across the European Economic Area, including the UK, with fines of up to 4%…
P0068.byline: By Kwontified. Published May 25, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0068.body:
The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation takes effect today, May 25, 2018, across the European Economic Area, including the UK, with fines of up to 4% of global annual turnover or EUR 20 million, whichever is greater, for the most serious breaches, according to a briefing by law firm HFW.

What happened

The transition period is over. From today, national data protection authorities can enforce the regulation, including the higher fines, and complaints from consumers can start the process.

Consent has to be provable. Customer lists remain usable after May 25 where consent was validly obtained, a McGuireWoods note for retailers said on May 10. The burden is on the business to show how, when and to what each person agreed.

Some companies acted early. The UK pub chain JD Wetherspoon told customers in June 2017 that it would stop sending email newsletters and delete its email database, MediaPost reported, saying the emails could be seen as intrusive.

Why it matters for brands

A list’s value now depends on its records. Addresses without documented consent cannot safely be used for marketing to people in the EU, so a brand’s mailable list may be much smaller than its database.

Data from every channel is covered. Customer data a brand collects through its own site, loyalty programs, events or partners all falls under the rules when it concerns people in the EU.

Fines scale with the whole company. Because the ceiling is set as a share of global turnover, a breach in one European market can carry a penalty sized to the entire business. That makes European customer data a question for the leadership team, not only for the marketing department that collects most of it.

What to do now

  1. Stop marketing to European records that lack documented consent until counsel has reviewed them.
  2. Check every sign-up form and checkout box records the date, source and consent wording from today.
  3. Ask each agency and platform partner that handles your European customer data how it meets the regulation, and get the answer in writing.

P0083.title: Instagram adds shopping to Stories, starting with Adidas, Aritzia and Louis Vuitton
P0083.alt: A phone on a small flexible tripod beside white canvas sneakers on a white block against a pink wall.
P0083.ttag: Instagram adds shopping to Stories, starting with Adidas, Aritzia and Louis Vuitton | Kwontified
P0083.desc: Instagram said on June 12, 2018 that it is bringing shopping to Stories, letting businesses tag products in a story with a shopping-bag sticker that…
P0083.byline: By Kwontified. Published Jun 13, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0083.body:
Instagram said on June 12, 2018 that it is bringing shopping to Stories, letting businesses tag products in a story with a shopping-bag sticker that viewers tap to see the item and its price, according to Instagram’s announcement. The feature starts with a select group of brands, including Adidas, Aritzia and Louis Vuitton, with more to follow, Droid Life reported.

What happened

Shopping moves beyond the feed. Until now, product tags on Instagram appeared in feed posts, where a business could tag items in a photo and link each to a product page. The new sticker brings the same tag into Stories, the full-screen posts that disappear after 24 hours.

The flow is short. A viewer taps the shopping-bag sticker, sees the product’s details and price, and can continue to the brand’s website to buy, The Drum reported. The purchase itself still happens off Instagram.

Access is limited for now. Instagram described the launch as the start of expanding shopping beyond the feed, beginning with a small number of brands, and did not give a date for wider availability.

Why it matters for brands

Stories are where a brand’s most casual content lives: launches, behind-the-scenes clips, short demonstrations. Until now those posts could build interest but could not point to a product without a separate link. A tagged product turns a 15-second clip into a path to a product page.

The content requirement changes. A story that sells needs the product in frame, a clear reason to tap and a product page that matches what the viewer just saw. Brands that already treat Stories as a creative afterthought will find the sticker exposes the gap.

The measurement question arrives early. Because the purchase happens on the brand’s site, Instagram’s numbers will show taps and visits, while sales sit in the brand’s own analytics. Brands that want to know what Stories sell will need tracking links in place before the feature reaches them.

What to do now

  1. If you already use product tags in feed posts, confirm your product catalog on Instagram is complete and priced correctly, since Stories tags will draw on the same products.
  2. Plan two or three stories a month built around a single product, so you are ready when the sticker reaches your account.
  3. Add campaign tracking to the product pages you tag, so that Instagram visits can be matched to orders in your own analytics.

P0080.title: Supreme Court lets states require out-of-state online sellers to collect sales tax
P0080.alt: Five colorful mailboxes on a lilac wall above a string-tied brown paper parcel on the sidewalk.
P0080.ttag: Supreme Court lets states require out-of-state online sellers to collect sales tax | Kwontified
P0080.desc: The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 on June 21, 2018, in South Dakota v.
P0080.byline: By Kwontified. Published Jun 22, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0080.body:
The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 on June 21, 2018, in South Dakota v. Wayfair that a state can require an out-of-state seller with no physical presence there to collect its sales tax, overruling the physical-presence rule of Quill Corp. v. North Dakota (1992), according to the Court’s opinion as summarized by SCOTUSblog. Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote for the majority.

What happened

The physical-presence rule is gone. Since 1992, a state could make a retailer collect sales tax only if the retailer had a store, warehouse or staff in that state. The Court said that test was incorrect for an economy in which sellers reach customers everywhere online, and also overruled the 1967 Bellas Hess decision on which Quill rested.

South Dakota’s law was the test case. It requires sellers to collect the state’s sales tax if, in a year, they deliver more than $100,000 of goods or services into South Dakota or complete 200 or more separate transactions there, and the Court found that the sellers in the case, Wayfair, Overstock.com and Newegg, had a substantial nexus with the state through their economic and virtual contacts, according to an alert from law firm Faegre Baker Daniels. The opinion cited estimates that states lose between $8 billion and $33 billion a year in uncollected tax.

Four justices dissented. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that Congress, not the Court, should change the rule.

Markets reacted the same day. Overstock.com shares fell about 7% and Etsy’s 1.6%, according to Associated Press figures; Wayfair said it did not expect a noticeable effect on its business, and Overstock warned the ruling could hurt small business innovation on the internet.

Why it matters for brands

Collection obligations can now follow sales, not buildings. A brand selling direct to consumers from one state may soon owe collection in every state that adopts a law like South Dakota’s, once it passes that state’s thresholds.

Marketplaces were already moving. Amazon has collected sales tax on its own sales in every state with a sales tax since April 1, 2017, CNN reported, and under state marketplace laws it began collecting on behalf of third-party sellers in Washington from January 1, 2018, Avalara noted. Expect more states to put the duty on marketplaces rather than on each seller.

Price comparisons will narrow. Where an out-of-state seller’s price looked lower because no tax was added at checkout, that gap will close as states act.

What to do now

  1. Pull a 12-month report of your direct-to-consumer and marketplace orders by destination state, counting both dollars and transactions.
  2. Mark every state where you exceed $100,000 or 200 transactions, since South Dakota’s thresholds are the model other states are most likely to copy.
  3. Ask your tax adviser which states have laws ready to take effect and which marketplaces will collect on your behalf, and budget for a sales tax system before the first state’s law applies. This is not legal or tax advice.

P0081.crumb: Amazon sets Prime Day 2018 for July 16, a…
P0081.title: Amazon sets Prime Day 2018 for July 16, a 36-hour event in 17 countries
P0081.alt: Stacked cardboard boxes topped with a striped towel beside potted red geraniums on a stone step by a blue wall.
P0081.ttag: Amazon sets Prime Day 2018 for July 16, a 36-hour event in 17 countries | Kwontified
P0081.desc: Amazon announced on July 3, 2018 that Prime Day will start on July 16 at 12 p.m. Pacific (3 p.m.
P0081.byline: By Kwontified. Published Jul 5, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0081.body:
Amazon announced on July 3, 2018 that Prime Day will start on July 16 at 12 p.m. Pacific (3 p.m. Eastern) and run through July 17, a 36-hour event with more than one million deals for Prime members worldwide, according to Amazon’s announcement. Last year’s event ran 30 hours.

What happened

The event is longer and starts midday. Prime Day 2018 opens on a Monday afternoon in the US and runs into Tuesday, six hours longer than 2017, Retail TouchPoints reported.

It reaches more countries. Prime Day runs in 17 countries, adding Australia, Singapore, the Netherlands and Luxembourg to the US, UK, Canada, Mexico, Spain, Italy, Germany, France, Japan, India, China, Belgium and Austria, according to Amazon.

Amazon’s own products are front and center. Amazon promised 50% more Spotlight Deals than last year and its biggest deals yet on Alexa-enabled devices, 9to5Mac reported.

The date matches a banner that appeared briefly on Amazon’s UK site on June 21, which Amazon had not confirmed at the time.

Why it matters for brands

The day has a new shape. A noon Pacific start puts the opening hours in the US afternoon and the second half across a full Tuesday, so the busiest hours, and the moments when advertising budgets run out, will not match last year’s pattern.

Amazon’s devices will compete for the same attention. With Amazon promoting its own hardware hard, the event’s most visible placements will carry Amazon products, and brand deals will rely more on search and category pages to be found.

Stock timing is now fixed. Inventory meant for the event needs to be in Amazon’s warehouses and sellable before July 16, and brands now have a firm date to plan replenishment and the days after.

What to do now

  1. Set event budgets for two calendar days, with the largest share on Tuesday, July 17, and a rule for raising budgets during the afternoon of July 16.
  2. Confirm that deal products and the products shoppers browse next are in stock in Amazon’s warehouses, and check inbound shipments due before July 16.
  3. Schedule hourly checks of spend, stock and Buy Box status from 12 p.m. Pacific on July 16 to the end of July 17, with one named owner.

P0094.crumb: Prime Day 2018, early read: sales ran…
P0094.title: Prime Day 2018, early read: sales ran ahead of 2017 after a broken first hour
P0094.alt: Red hand cart stacked with taped cardboard shipping boxes against a weathered blue wall.
P0094.ttag: Prime Day 2018, early read: sales ran ahead of 2017 after a broken first hour | Kwontified
P0094.desc: Prime Day 2018 ended at midnight Pacific on July 17, and the first public figures, from Amazon’s own statements and from one seller-software firm, point…
P0094.byline: By Kwontified. Published Jul 18, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0094.body:
Prime Day 2018 ended at midnight Pacific on July 17, and the first public figures, from Amazon’s own statements and from one seller-software firm, point to sales well ahead of 2017 despite a site failure in the event’s opening minutes. Amazon has not yet published totals, so every number here is preliminary and partial.

What happened

The start broke. Amazon’s 36-hour event opened at noon Pacific (3 p.m. Eastern) on July 16, and shoppers who clicked through to deals were met with error pages. Amazon said that afternoon that some customers were having difficulty shopping and that it was working to resolve the issue quickly, adding that many were shopping successfully, Fortune reported.

Amazon says the first hours still grew. In a statement on July 17, Amazon said customers ordered more items in the first hour than in the first hour of Prime Day 2017, and that sales in the first 10 hours grew faster than in the same period last year, as reported on July 17. It gave no dollar figures.

One outside reading agrees. Feedvisor, which sells pricing software to Amazon sellers, said its clients’ sales in the first 12 hours rose 89% over the first 12 hours of 2017, with orders up 69%, while sales in the first hour fell 5%, Bloomberg reported. Feedvisor sees only its own clients, not Amazon’s totals.

The benchmark to beat is $3.4 billion. Coresight Research forecast in June that Prime Day 2018 would bring in about $3.4 billion worldwide, against an estimated $2.4 billion in 2017, in its preview.

Why it matters for brands

The outage moved demand rather than removing it. If the first hour was weak and the next eleven were strong, shoppers who hit errors came back. Brands that capped ad budgets by the hour, or pulled spending in the first hour, may have run out of budget in the hours when shoppers returned.

Early figures describe the event, not the brand. An 89% rise across one software firm’s clients says little about any one category, and Amazon’s own claims cover items and growth rates, not revenue. The full picture needs Amazon’s recap and each brand’s own reports.

The halo is still unmeasured. Sales after the event, at full price on Amazon and at other retailers that ran their own July 17 sales, will decide how much of Prime Day was new demand.

What to do now

  1. Pull hourly sales and ad spend for July 16 and 17 before the reports roll up into daily totals, and mark when each campaign hit its budget cap.
  2. Record the deal price, units sold and ad cost of every Lightning Deal and Deal of the Day while the data is fresh.
  3. Keep a two-week baseline of sales and organic rank after the event, so the lift can be separated from sales the event pulled forward.

P0115.crumb: Amazon unifies AMS, AMG and AAP as Amazon…
P0115.title: Amazon unifies AMS, AMG and AAP as Amazon Advertising; Headline Search Ads become Sponsored Brands
P0115.alt: Empty wooden picture frame and a twine-tied cardboard parcel leaning against a sunlit mustard-yellow wall.
P0115.ttag: Amazon unifies AMS, AMG and AAP as Amazon Advertising; Headline Search Ads become Sponsored Brands | Kwontified
P0115.desc: Amazon said on September 5, 2018 that it is bringing its three advertising businesses under one name, Amazon Advertising, and retiring the names Amazon…
P0115.byline: By Kwontified. Published Sep 6, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0115.body:
Amazon said on September 5, 2018 that it is bringing its three advertising businesses under one name, Amazon Advertising, and retiring the names Amazon Media Group (AMG), Amazon Marketing Services (AMS) and the Amazon Advertising Platform (AAP), according to Amazon’s announcement. Two products change names with it: Headline Search Ads become Sponsored Brands, and the Amazon Advertising Platform becomes the Amazon DSP.

What happened

One brand replaces three. Until now, AMS ran the self-service search ads sold through its console, AAP was the programmatic buying platform, and AMG sold Amazon’s display and media packages to brands and agencies. Amazon said it is retiring all three names in favor of Amazon Advertising.

Two formats get new names. Headline Search Ads, the banner with a brand’s logo and custom headline above search results, is now Sponsored Brands, which Amazon said better describes a keyword-targeted ad that sits beside Sponsored Products. The Amazon Advertising Platform is now the Amazon DSP (demand-side platform), the tool for buying display and video ads programmatically.

The products themselves are unchanged. The rename does not change how the ad products work or how Amazon’s advertising teams are organized, AdExchanger reported, and the console that AMS advertisers use still runs cost-per-click campaigns for Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands. Digiday first reported in early August that Amazon planned to consolidate the three businesses, Marketing Dive noted.

Why it matters for brands

The vocabulary in every plan and report changes now. Agencies, Amazon account teams and Amazon’s own help pages can be expected to move to the new names over the coming months, so a brand’s budgets, dashboards and contracts that still say AMS or Headline Search Ads will drift out of step with the reports it receives.

Search ads and display now sit under one roof. A single advertising brand makes it easier for Amazon to sell search, display and video together, and brands that bought them from different teams should expect proposals that bundle them.

Nothing in the auction has moved. Bids, budgets, keyword targeting and reporting for Sponsored Products and the renamed Sponsored Brands work as they did on September 4, so there is no reason to change a campaign because of the announcement alone.

What to do now

  1. Update internal plans, dashboards and agency briefs to the new names: Amazon Advertising, Sponsored Brands and the Amazon DSP.
  2. List which teams or agencies buy your Amazon search ads, DSP and any media packages, and who reports on each, before bundled proposals arrive.
  3. Leave live campaigns unchanged unless performance, not the rename, calls for it.

P0140.crumb: Amazon starts its Black Friday deals on…
P0140.title: Amazon starts its Black Friday deals on November 16, a week before Black Friday
P0140.alt: A stack of twine-tied kraft parcels beside a small potted fir tree against a green wall.
P0140.ttag: Amazon starts its Black Friday deals on November 16, a week before Black Friday | Kwontified
P0140.desc: Amazon said on November 15, 2018 that its Black Friday deals start on Friday, November 16, a week before Black Friday itself, with more than 50 Deals of…
P0140.byline: By Kwontified. Published Nov 16, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0140.body:
Amazon said on November 15, 2018 that its Black Friday deals start on Friday, November 16, a week before Black Friday itself, with more than 50 Deals of the Day during the event, Amazon said. The announcement sets the shape of Cyber Week 2018: Black Friday falls on November 23 and Cyber Monday on November 26, but Amazon’s own event is now more than a week long.

What happened

Amazon opened the calendar early. Its Black Friday deals week begins on November 16 and runs through Black Friday, November 23, with deals in every department, according to Amazon’s announcement.

Walmart had already set its dates. On November 8, Walmart said most of its Black Friday deals will go live on Walmart.com at 10 p.m. ET on November 21, the day before Thanksgiving and two hours earlier than in prior years, with in-store deals starting at 6 p.m. on Thanksgiving, Fortune reported.

Shipping is part of the offer. Amazon has given every US customer free shipping with no minimum on orders arriving by Christmas since November 5, Amazon said, and Target is offering free two-day shipping with no minimum from November 1 through December 22, CNBC reported.

Why it matters for brands

On Amazon, Cyber Week now runs for more than a week. Shoppers will see deal pages from November 16, so a brand whose products, prices and advertising are timed only for Black Friday and Cyber Monday will meet a week of competitors’ deals with its regular offer.

Advertising will get busier earlier. Deal traffic and the advertisers chasing it arrive from November 16, so click prices can climb before the weekend most budgets are built around.

Walmart’s start time moves online demand to Wednesday night. Brands selling on Walmart.com should expect a spike on the evening of November 21, before most teams are watching.

What to do now

  1. Check today which of your products have confirmed deals between November 16 and November 26, and when each one runs.
  2. Raise daily budgets on your best-converting campaigns from November 16, not November 23, and set a cost-per-click ceiling for each important search.
  3. Put someone on watch for the evening of November 21 for Walmart.com and for each Amazon deal window, with authority to change bids and budgets.

P0151.crumb: Early read, Cyber Week 2018: Black Friday…
P0151.title: Early read, Cyber Week 2018: Black Friday online sales rose 23.6% to $6.22 billion (preliminary)
P0151.alt: Blue, red and orange paper shopping bags lined up on a weathered wooden bench against a sunlit cream wall.
P0151.ttag: Early read, Cyber Week 2018: Black Friday online sales rose 23.6% to $6.22 billion (preliminary) | Kwontified
P0151.desc: Preliminary: US shoppers spent a record $6.22 billion online on Black Friday, November 23, up 23.6% from 2017, according to Adobe Analytics, Marketing…
P0151.byline: By Kwontified. Published Nov 27, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0151.body:
Preliminary: US shoppers spent a record $6.22 billion online on Black Friday, November 23, up 23.6% from 2017, according to Adobe Analytics, Marketing Land reported on November 26. Thanksgiving Day brought a record $3.7 billion, TechCrunch reported, up 28%, and Adobe said on Cyber Monday, November 26, that it expected the day to reach about $7.8 billion, as reported. These are early figures from one tracker, published before Cyber Monday closed.

What happened

Online growth beat the forecasts. Adobe had forecast Black Friday at $5.9 billion and Cyber Monday at $7.7 billion when it published its season outlook on November 1. Black Friday came in above that, and Adobe raised its Cyber Monday estimate on the day.

Phones did more of the buying. Black Friday was the first day with more than $2 billion of US online sales on smartphones, and smartphones accounted for 33.5% of online sales, up from 29.1% a year earlier, according to Adobe’s figures as reported by Marketing Land.

Small Business Saturday brought $3.02 billion online, up 25.5%, Adobe said, according to the same TechCrunch report.

Final figures for Cyber Monday and the full weekend, from Adobe and other trackers, were not available at the time of writing.

Why it matters for brands

The weekend is running ahead of plan for the market as a whole. Online growth near 24% on Black Friday sits at or above the top of the 17% to 22% range Deloitte gave for holiday e-commerce in September, so a brand whose own sales grew less than that lost share over the weekend, even if its total looks strong.

Mobile is now a third of the biggest days. A product page that reads poorly on a phone, with a truncated title or images that do not answer basic questions, was shown to more shoppers this weekend than ever.

What to do now

  1. Pull your own Black Friday and Thanksgiving results against the same days in 2017 and compare the growth with Adobe’s 23.6% and 28%.
  2. Split the weekend’s sales and ad spend by device where your reporting allows, and check how the phone share compares with Adobe’s 33.5%.
  3. Record today’s preliminary numbers next to your pre-season forecast, then update them when final Cyber Monday figures arrive, so the December review grades the plan rather than the memory of the weekend.

P0176.crumb: Amazon cuts referral fees on low-priced…
P0176.title: Amazon cuts referral fees on low-priced items and raises most FBA fees, effective February 19
P0176.alt: A brass hanging balance scale tips with a stack of coins on one pan and a twine-tied parcel on the other.
P0176.ttag: Amazon cuts referral fees on low-priced items and raises most FBA fees, effective February 19 | Kwontified
P0176.desc: Amazon told sellers on December 19, 2018 that it will cut referral fees on low-priced products in several categories and raise Fulfillment by Amazon fees…
P0176.byline: By Kwontified. Published Dec 20, 2018. 2-minute read.
P0176.body:
Amazon told sellers on December 19, 2018 that it will cut referral fees on low-priced products in several categories and raise Fulfillment by Amazon fees for most size tiers, with both changes taking effect on February 19, 2019, according to its notice in Seller Forums. Storage fee changes start earlier, on February 15, Viral Launch reported the same day.

What happened

Cheap items pay less to sell. The referral fee for Beauty, Health & Personal Care and Baby (excluding baby apparel) falls from 15% to 8% on items priced at $10 or less, and Grocery & Gourmet pays 8% on items at $15 or less. Furniture pays 10% instead of 15% on the part of the price above $200, and Jewelry pays 5% instead of 20% on the part above $250, according to the notice.

The minimum fee drops sharply. The per-item minimum referral fee falls from $1.00 to $0.30 in most categories, and from $2.00 to $0.30 for jewelry and watches, a move Business Insider reported as an effort to widen selection.

Fulfillment costs more for most products. FBA fees do not change for small and large standard-size items with a shipping weight of 10 ounces or less, and rise for other size tiers. Amazon said it expects more than 40% of FBA units shipped to see no change or a decrease.

Storage gets cheaper for slow stock. From February 15, Amazon will stop charging long-term storage fees on units stored 181 to 365 days, and the minimum long-term fee for units stored more than a year falls from $0.50 to $0.15 per unit.

Why it matters for brands

The low-price shelf just reopened. At a $1.00 minimum, a $5 item paid a 20% referral fee; at $0.30 it pays the category rate. Brands that kept small sizes, refills and add-on items off Amazon because the fee made them unprofitable should look again.

The gains and losses sit in different products. A $9 beauty item gains from the 8% rate, while a two-pound product shipped by FBA pays more to fulfill. Most catalogs will see both, so the net effect depends on the mix.

Advertising ceilings move with the fees. The amount a brand can spend on advertising for each sale rises where fees fall and shrinks where they rise.

What to do now

  1. Re-run unit margins for every Amazon product using the February 19 referral and FBA fees.
  2. List products priced at $10 or less in Beauty, Health & Personal Care and Baby, and $15 or less in Grocery, and test whether they now earn a profit on Amazon.
  3. Reset the maximum advertising cost per sale for each product whose margin changes, before February 19.

P0192.title: Target launches Target+, an invite-only marketplace on Target.com
P0192.alt: A white shopping cart holding a knit blanket, vases and a potted plant against a sunlit red wall.
P0192.ttag: Target launches Target+, an invite-only marketplace on Target.com | Kwontified
P0192.desc: Target launched Target+ on February 25, 2019, adding products from third-party sellers to Target.com, according to Target’s announcement .
P0192.byline: By Kwontified. Published Feb 26, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0192.body:
Target launched Target+ on February 25, 2019, adding products from third-party sellers to Target.com, according to Target’s announcement. Unlike the marketplaces on Amazon and Walmart.com, where brands apply to sell, Target+ is by invitation: Target selects specialty and national brands and asks them to join, CNBC reported.

What happened

Target picks the sellers. “This is intended to be a very curated and select group of products and brands,” Rick Gomez, Target’s chief marketing and digital officer, told CNBC, adding that Target is reaching out to the brands it wants. Over the past few months Target tested the approach with Mizuno, Kaplan and Casio, according to CNBC, and the program is in its early stages.

Shoppers keep Target’s promises. Target+ items appear throughout Target.com rather than in a separate section, and guests get 5% off with a REDcard, free shipping and in-store returns, Target said. The third-party sellers handle shipping and other costs, CNBC reported.

The categories follow search. Target highlighted running shoes, patio accessories, STEM learning toys, musical instruments and baseball gear. Gomez told CNBC the categories were chosen from research into what guests search for on Target.com, and that home goods, electronics and outdoor gear may follow.

Why it matters for brands

A third US marketplace has opened with a different gate. On Amazon and Walmart.com the question is whether a brand chooses to sell; on Target+ it is whether Target chooses the brand. Being invited depends on filling a gap Target can see in its own search data.

The promise belongs to Target, and the work belongs to the seller. Free shipping and in-store returns are Target’s commitments to the guest, but the seller ships the order and bears the cost, so a brand’s fulfillment speed and returns handling become part of Target’s customer experience.

The stakes are growing. Target’s digital sales rose 29% during the 2018 holiday season, CNBC reported, so a place in its online assortment carries more weight each quarter.

What to do now

  1. Search Target.com for your category’s most common terms and note where results are thin; those are the gaps Target says it is filling.
  2. If you already sell to Target wholesale, ask your buyer how Target+ will treat items outside your current assortment.
  3. Check whether you could ship Target+ orders on your own at Target’s free-shipping standard and absorb in-store returns, before an invitation arrives.

P0195.title: Amazon launches Project Zero, letting brands remove counterfeit listings themselves
P0195.alt: Clear corked bottle on a white paper backdrop with color swatch cards, a tape measure and a round mirror.
P0195.ttag: Amazon launches Project Zero, letting brands remove counterfeit listings themselves | Kwontified
P0195.desc: Amazon launched Project Zero on February 28, 2019, a program that lets brands remove counterfeit listings from its stores without first contacting Amazon,…
P0195.byline: By Kwontified. Published Mar 1, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0195.body:
Amazon launched Project Zero on February 28, 2019, a program that lets brands remove counterfeit listings from its stores without first contacting Amazon, according to Amazon’s announcement. The program is invite-only and US-only at launch, and brands need a government-registered trademark and enrollment in Amazon Brand Registry, TechCrunch reported.

What happened

Project Zero has three parts. Automated protections use the logos, trademarks and other brand data that brands supply to scan Amazon’s stores and remove suspected counterfeits; Amazon said it scans more than 5 billion product listing updates a day and that, in testing, the protections stopped on average 100 times more suspected counterfeits than it removed in response to brand reports. A self-service tool lets brands take down counterfeit listings directly. Product serialization puts a unique code on every unit at manufacture, which Amazon scans to verify each unit before it reaches a customer.

The tools come with conditions. Enrollment is free, and serialization costs $0.01 to $0.05 per unit depending on volume, according to TechCrunch. Amazon will monitor brands’ self-service removals, and its FAQ says brands “must maintain a high bar for accuracy in order to maintain their Project Zero privileges.”

Until now, a brand that found a counterfeit had to report it and wait for Amazon to investigate.

Why it matters for brands

The removal button moves to the brand. A brand that is enrolled can act on a counterfeit the day it finds one, without a case and a wait. That puts the speed of enforcement in the hands of whoever at the brand watches the listings.

The trademark is the entry ticket. Without a registered trademark and Brand Registry, a brand cannot apply, so brands still waiting on a trademark filing remain on the old report-and-wait process.

The privilege can be lost. Because Amazon ties continued access to accurate removals, a brand that uses the tool against authorized resellers or price competitors rather than genuine fakes risks losing it. The tool removes counterfeits, not unwanted sellers.

What to do now

  1. Confirm your trademark registration and Brand Registry enrollment, and sign up to be considered for Project Zero.
  2. Decide who at the brand will review listings and use the removal tool, and write down what counts as a counterfeit before anyone presses the button.
  3. Price serialization for your most-copied products: at $0.01 to $0.05 a unit, set the cost against the sales and reviews those products lose to fakes.

P0198.crumb: Amazon halts weekly orders to smaller…
P0198.title: Amazon halts weekly orders to smaller vendors and points them to Seller Central
P0198.alt: An open cardboard box spilling kraft packing paper beside a roll of tape on a sunlit wooden bench.
P0198.ttag: Amazon halts weekly orders to smaller vendors and points them to Seller Central | Kwontified
P0198.desc: Amazon stopped sending weekly purchase orders to a large group of smaller Vendor Central suppliers on Monday, March 4, 2019, and told some of them that…
P0198.byline: By Kwontified. Published Mar 7, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0198.body:
Amazon stopped sending weekly purchase orders to a large group of smaller Vendor Central suppliers on Monday, March 4, 2019, and told some of them that the change was permanent and that they should sell as third-party sellers instead, Digiday reported in a story republished by its sister site Modern Retail on March 6. Agency executives put the number of affected vendors in the thousands.

What happened

The orders stopped without notice. Vendors who normally receive a replenishment order from Amazon each week received none on Monday, according to Amazon-focused agency executives quoted in the report. The affected vendors were described as businesses selling $10 million or less a year on Amazon, without an assigned vendor manager.

The explanations changed within a day. On Monday, some vendors received an automated reply calling the missing orders a technical glitch. On Tuesday, thousands of others were told that the move was permanent and that their businesses would do better on Amazon’s third-party marketplace, the report said.

Amazon did not describe a program. A spokesperson said the company regularly reviews its selling partner relationships and “may make changes when we see an opportunity to provide customers with improved selection, value and convenience,” and said there is no existing program called “One Vendor,” the name agencies had used for a rumored combined system for first-party and third-party suppliers. Separately, Amazon has told vendors who ship orders directly to customers on its behalf that their drop-ship accounts are being suspended, EcommerceBytes reported on March 5.

Why it matters for brands

The risk sits with the brands that depend on one buyer. A vendor that ships to Amazon wholesale does not control its price, its listing or its timing; Amazon does. When the order stops, the brand’s Amazon sales stop with it until the products are relisted under a seller account.

Moving to Seller Central changes the economics, not only the paperwork. As a seller, the brand sets its price, pays a referral fee on each sale and either ships the orders itself or pays for Fulfillment by Amazon. It also takes on the advertising, customer service and inventory planning that Amazon’s retail team did before.

The details are still moving. Amazon has not published a policy, and vendors received different messages on different days, so brands should treat this week’s reports as a warning rather than a settled rule.

What to do now

  1. Check this week’s purchase orders against the usual pattern, and ask your Amazon contact in writing whether your account is affected.
  2. Open or reactivate a Seller Central account and enroll your brand in Brand Registry now, so you can list and control your products if the orders do not return.
  3. Calculate your margin as a seller on your top products, using the referral fee and fulfillment cost, before deciding which ones to move.

P0205.title: Instagram launches Checkout, letting US shoppers buy from 20-plus brands in the app
P0205.alt: A phone on a small flexible tripod beside white canvas sneakers on a white block against a pink wall.
P0205.ttag: Instagram launches Checkout, letting US shoppers buy from 20-plus brands in the app | Kwontified
P0205.desc: Instagram launched Checkout on March 19, 2019, a closed beta that lets shoppers in the US buy products from more than 20 brands without leaving the app,…
P0205.byline: By Kwontified. Published Mar 20, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0205.body:
Instagram launched Checkout on March 19, 2019, a closed beta that lets shoppers in the US buy products from more than 20 brands without leaving the app, according to Instagram’s announcement. The launch brands include Adidas, Burberry, Dior, H&M, MAC Cosmetics, Nike, Uniqlo, Warby Parker and Zara, and they are rolling out over the coming weeks.

What happened

The purchase moves inside Instagram. On a brand’s shopping post, a shopper taps through to the product page and then a “Checkout on Instagram” button, chooses a size or color and pays in the app, according to the announcement. Name, email, billing details and shipping address are entered once and saved for later purchases, and shipping and delivery notifications arrive in Instagram.

Payments run through PayPal, and shoppers can pay with PayPal or major cards, TechCrunch reported. Sellers will pay for it. “We will introduce a selling fee,” an Instagram spokesperson told TechCrunch, adding that the fee is being tested with merchants in the beta; the amount was not disclosed. Until now, buying meant leaving Instagram for the retailer’s site in a browser, Fortune noted. TechCrunch put the number of people who tap product tags on shopping posts at 130 million.

The beta is limited. Instagram said Checkout is in closed beta for businesses, and Fortune counted 23 retailers at launch, noting that Instagram expects the list to grow.

Why it matters for brands

The sale and the customer data move with the checkout. When a shopper buys on a brand’s website, the brand runs the cart and sees the whole visit. Inside Instagram, the order and the payment details pass through Instagram and PayPal, and the brand pays a fee whose size Instagram has not disclosed.

Discovery and purchase are joining up. Shopping posts already let people find products on Instagram; a saved address and one-tap payment make it a place where they finish buying, which changes how a brand should measure its posts.

Most brands cannot use it yet. Checkout is invitation-only and US-only for now, so the brands outside the first group have time to decide whether they want in.

What to do now

  1. Check that your product catalog and shopping tags on Instagram are complete, since Checkout starts from a tagged shopping post.
  2. Ask your Facebook or Instagram partner contact how brands join the beta and what the selling fee will be, in writing.
  3. Compare the fee, once known, with what a website sale costs you after payment processing and ad spend, before moving traffic away from your own checkout.

P0222.crumb: Amazon plans to make free one-day…
P0222.title: Amazon plans to make free one-day shipping the Prime standard
P0222.alt: Red hand cart stacked with taped cardboard shipping boxes against a weathered blue wall.
P0222.ttag: Amazon plans to make free one-day shipping the Prime standard | Kwontified
P0222.desc: Amazon plans to make free one-day shipping the standard for Prime members and will spend about $800 million in the second quarter of 2019 to start, its…
P0222.byline: By Kwontified. Published Apr 26, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0222.body:
Amazon plans to make free one-day shipping the standard for Prime members and will spend about $800 million in the second quarter of 2019 to start, its chief financial officer, Brian Olsavsky, said on the company’s first-quarter earnings call on April 25, CNN reported. Prime has been built on free two-day shipping since it launched.

What happened

“Our goal is to evolve the two-day free shipping program into the one-day free shipping program,” Olsavsky said. Amazon already offers one-day delivery on some items, but it is not standard for all of them, and Olsavsky did not say when it would be. He said Amazon expects to “make steady progress quickly and through the year.”

The plan arrived with strong results. Net sales rose 17% to $59.7 billion in the first quarter and net income rose to $3.6 billion, Amazon reported. Its guidance for second-quarter operating income, $2.6 billion to $3.6 billion against $3.0 billion a year earlier, leaves room for the delivery spending. The release also noted that Amazon Day, which lets Prime members choose a weekly delivery day, is now available to all US Prime members.

Why it matters for brands

The delivery promise is about to tighten. A product that reaches a Prime shopper in two days today will be competing against products that arrive in one, and the delivery date sits beside the price on every product page.

Inventory placement matters more. Next-day delivery depends on stock sitting close to the shopper, so brands using Fulfillment by Amazon may find that how much stock they send, and when, affects which offers qualify for the faster promise.

Sellers who fulfil Prime orders themselves face the hardest test. A brand that ships its own Prime orders from one warehouse would need to reach most of the country overnight to keep pace.

What to do now

  1. List your top products by Prime sales and check which already show one-day delivery to major metro areas.
  2. Review FBA inventory levels on those products before the second-quarter replenishment cycle, so stock is not the reason an offer misses the faster promise.
  3. If you fulfil Prime orders yourself, cost out what overnight delivery to your main markets would add per order before Amazon publishes its new standard.

P0246.crumb: Amazon sets Prime Day 2019 for July 15…
P0246.title: Amazon sets Prime Day 2019 for July 15 and 16, its first 48-hour event
P0246.alt: Stacked cardboard boxes topped with a striped towel beside potted red geraniums on a stone step by a blue wall.
P0246.ttag: Amazon sets Prime Day 2019 for July 15 and 16, its first 48-hour event | Kwontified
P0246.desc: Amazon said on June 25, 2019 that Prime Day will start on Monday, July 15 and run for 48 hours through Tuesday, July 16, the first time the event has…
P0246.byline: By Kwontified. Published Jun 26, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0246.body:
Amazon said on June 25, 2019 that Prime Day will start on Monday, July 15 and run for 48 hours through Tuesday, July 16, the first time the event has lasted two days, according to its announcement. Prime Day 2018 ran 36 hours. Amazon promised more than one million deals for Prime members across 18 countries.

What happened

The event is a third longer. Moving from 36 to 48 hours gives shoppers two full days of deals, and Amazon called it its longest Prime Day, Retail Dive reported. The United Arab Emirates joins the list of 18 countries for the first time, according to Amazon.

Deals start before the event. Amazon opened early offers on the day of the announcement, including $120 off a Toshiba 43-inch Fire TV Edition television through June 30, and Whole Foods Market will run exclusive savings for Prime members, Retail Dive said. Shoppers without Prime can join through a 30-day free trial.

Sellers have a late door in. Amazon has opened Prime Exclusive Discounts to sellers that use Fulfillment by Amazon, ChannelX reported on June 20. For Prime Day, the discount must be at least 20% off the seller’s price and beat the product’s lowest price of the past 30 days, products need a rating of at least three stars or no rating, and discounts can be submitted until July 5, Feedvisor reported.

Why it matters for brands

Budgets built for 36 hours will run short. Ad budgets, deal quantities and stock plans sized for a day and a half now have to cover two full days, and the deal slots were settled before anyone knew the length: the deadline to apply for Lightning Deals passed on May 10, Feedvisor noted in May.

Other retailers will answer. Walmart and Target “will react, further turning up the competitive heat,” Moody’s analyst Charlie O’Shea told Retail Dive. Brands that sell across retailers should expect competing events in the same week and plan prices for all of them together.

The new discount program changes who can take part. Sellers that missed the Lightning Deal deadline can still offer a Prime Day price, but only on stock already in Amazon’s warehouses and only at a depth that beats their own recent low.

What to do now

  1. Re-cut Prime Day advertising budgets over 48 hours, with a second-day reserve, and raise daily caps on the products carrying deals.
  2. Decide by July 5 which FBA products can take a Prime Exclusive Discount of at least 20% that beats their 30-day low, and submit them.
  3. Check that deal quantities and stock in Amazon’s warehouses will last both days, and agree prices for any Walmart or Target events that week before July 15.

P0258.title: Prime Day 2019 closes after 48 hours; compare it by the hour
P0258.alt: An open cardboard box spilling kraft packing paper beside a roll of tape on a sunlit wooden bench.
P0258.ttag: Prime Day 2019 closes after 48 hours; compare it by the hour | Kwontified
P0258.byline: By Kwontified. Published Jul 17, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0258.body:
Prime Day 2019 closed at 11:59 p.m. Pacific time on July 16 after 48 hours, the longest Amazon has run, for Prime members in 18 countries, as Amazon announced in June. Final results are not public yet. This early read is preliminary: it sets out what was known by the end of the event and what brands should check before the official numbers arrive.

What happened

The event ran longer than before. Amazon started Prime Day at midnight Pacific time on July 15 and ran it for 48 hours, up from 36 hours in 2018, with deals at Whole Foods Market and early offers that began in June.

Rivals ran alongside it. Target held Deal Days on July 15 and 16 with no membership required and early-access deals of up to 50% off some kitchen items, and eBay ran a three-week sale from July 1 with a “Crash Sale” on July 15, CBS News reported on July 8. Walmart’s own online event runs from July 14 to 17, Techlicious reported.

The first numbers came on July 16, from Amazon and from Adobe. Amazon said Prime members in the US had saved hundreds of millions of dollars on day one, and that its sellers worldwide, mostly small and medium-sized businesses, had the biggest 24-hour sales day in Amazon history, in a mid-event update; it gave no sales total. Adobe Analytics, which tracks 80 of the top 100 US online retailers, said retailers with more than $1 billion in annual revenue sold 64% more online on the first day than on an average Monday, against a 54% lift during Prime Day 2018, and retailers with under $5 million in sales saw 30%, CNBC reported.

Why it matters for brands

The extra 12 hours changes the comparison. A brand comparing Prime Day 2019 with 2018 is comparing 48 hours with 36, so total event sales will rise even if hourly sales do not. The fair comparison is sales per hour, or the full week around the event against the same week in 2018.

The rival events blur the halo. With Target, eBay and Walmart discounting on the same days, a brand’s sales outside Amazon may rise or fall because of those events rather than Prime Day itself.

The days after matter as much as the event. Shoppers who bought on July 15 and 16 may have pulled forward purchases they would have made later in July, so the event’s net effect shows only once the following weeks are in.

What to do now

  1. Pull hourly sales, ad spend and sessions for July 15 and 16 before Amazon’s reports roll up into daily totals.
  2. Compare sales per event hour with Prime Day 2018, not the event total.
  3. Mark the four weeks after the event as the measurement window, and judge the event only once that window closes.

P0277.crumb: US 15% tariffs on $112 billion of Chinese…
P0277.title: US 15% tariffs on $112 billion of Chinese imports, including most clothing, take effect
P0277.alt: A shrink-wrapped pallet of cardboard boxes beside a yellow pallet jack against a gray wall.
P0277.ttag: US 15% tariffs on $112 billion of Chinese imports, including most clothing, take effect | Kwontified
P0277.desc: A 15% tariff on about $112 billion of Chinese imports took effect on Sunday, September 1, 2019, reaching clothing, shoes and other consumer goods that…
P0277.byline: By Kwontified. Published Sep 2, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0277.body:
A 15% tariff on about $112 billion of Chinese imports took effect on Sunday, September 1, 2019, reaching clothing, shoes and other consumer goods that earlier rounds of the trade dispute had largely spared. The rate is higher than the 10% first announced: the Office of the US Trade Representative raised it to 15% ad valorem in a Federal Register notice published August 30, at the President’s direction, after China announced retaliatory tariffs.

What happened

The September 1 duties are the first part of a list of Chinese goods with an annual trade value of about $300 billion. On August 13, USTR moved some products to December 15, including cell phones, laptop computers, video game consoles, certain toys, computer monitors and certain footwear and clothing. The rest took effect on September 1, and the August 30 notice sets the December 15 rate at 15% as well.

The reach into consumer goods is new. With the September 1 round, 87% of textiles and clothing imported from China and 52% of shoes are subject to the tariffs, and more than two-thirds of US consumer goods imports from China face higher duties, the Associated Press reported.

More increases are scheduled. On August 23, after Beijing announced tariffs on $75 billion of US goods, the President said the 25% duty on $250 billion of Chinese imports already taxed would rise to 30% from October 1, CNBC reported.

Why it matters for brands

Apparel, footwear and accessories brands that make goods in China now pay the duty on stock landing for the fourth quarter. Because the tariff is charged on the import value, its effect on margin depends on how far the retail price sits above that value. Take a jacket with a $20 import value that sells for $80: a 15% duty adds $3.00 to its cost, about 4% of the retail price, which comes straight out of contribution margin unless the price moves.

The duty is paid by whoever imports the goods. A brand that imports and sells through its own Amazon or Walmart seller account decides alone whether to pass it on. A brand that imports and sells to a retailer as a vendor pays it too, but recovers it only if the retailer accepts a higher cost price.

The December 15 group buys time for some holiday stock, and only for products on that list.

What to do now

  1. Check each SKU’s tariff classification against the September 1 and December 15 lists and note which inbound shipments clear customs after September 1.
  2. Recalculate landed cost and contribution margin for affected products at 15%, and for goods already taxed at 25%, at 30% from October 1.
  3. Decide on any price changes before setting Q4 advertising targets, because the margin each sale can spend on ads falls with every dollar of duty.

P0305.crumb: Amazon held its first ad conference for…
P0305.title: Amazon held its first ad conference for brands, AdCon 2019, in Seattle
P0305.alt: Empty wooden folding chairs facing a lectern against a coral wall, with a blank lanyard badge hung on one chair.
P0305.ttag: Amazon held its first ad conference for brands, AdCon 2019, in Seattle | Kwontified
P0305.desc: Amazon held its first large advertising conference aimed at brands last week in Seattle, drawing about 400 people to a two-day, invite-only event called…
P0305.byline: By Kwontified. Published Oct 9, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0305.body:
Amazon held its first large advertising conference aimed at brands last week in Seattle, drawing about 400 people to a two-day, invite-only event called AdCon 2019, CNBC reported on October 8. Amazon declined to comment.

What happened

The program combined keynotes from Amazon’s senior advertising executives with breakout sessions on its ad products. Paul Kotas, senior vice president of Amazon Advertising, and Colleen Aubrey, vice president of performance advertising, took questions from attendees, according to CNBC. Brands including mattress maker Tuft & Needle and pet food company I and Love and You presented case studies. Other sessions covered reaching new customers, using sponsored ads, and practices for hardlines such as electronics and appliances, softlines such as clothing and linens, and consumables.

The audience is the change. Amazon’s ad event in 2018, Rev2018, was much smaller and aimed at agencies. AdCon was built for the brands themselves, and one sponsor told CNBC the attendees were mostly small and medium-sized companies, since large brands tend to have a dedicated Amazon representative. Another sponsor called it “a coming-out party for Amazon’s advertising team.”

The business behind it is large. Amazon’s advertising unit topped $10 billion in revenue in 2018, and eMarketer expects Amazon to account for about 10% of US digital ad spending in 2020, third behind Google and Facebook, CNBC noted. In the second quarter of 2019, Amazon’s “other” revenue line, mostly advertising, grew 37% to $3.0 billion, Amazon reported in July.

Why it matters for brands

Amazon is now selling its ad products to brand teams directly rather than mainly through agencies. That brings more training and more product pitches to the people who own the Amazon budget, and it also means more of the advice those teams hear comes from the seller of the media.

The session list shows where Amazon wants the spend to go: new customers and category-specific playbooks, alongside the sponsored ads most brands already buy. Brands should expect the fourth-quarter pitch from Amazon’s ad teams to lean on those themes.

What to do now

  1. Ask your Amazon representative or agency for the AdCon session materials relevant to your category, and note which recommendations would raise spend and which would change how it is measured.
  2. Before adding budget on Amazon’s advice, set the test you will use to judge it, such as new-to-brand sales against a holdout period.
  3. If you have no dedicated Amazon representative, treat events like this as the main way to hear about new ad products early, and ask to be invited to the next one.

P0309.crumb: Amazon sets Black Friday Deals Week for…
P0309.title: Amazon sets Black Friday Deals Week for November 22 to 29, with Cyber Monday deals on December 2
P0309.alt: A stack of twine-tied kraft parcels beside a small potted fir tree against a green wall.
P0309.ttag: Amazon sets Black Friday Deals Week for November 22 to 29, with Cyber Monday deals on December 2 | Kwontified
P0309.desc: Amazon will run its Black Friday Deals Week in the US from Friday, November 22 through Black Friday on November 29, with new deals “all day, every day,”…
P0309.byline: By Kwontified. Published Nov 19, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0309.body:
Amazon will run its Black Friday Deals Week in the US from Friday, November 22 through Black Friday on November 29, with new deals “all day, every day,” and one-time-only deals on Thanksgiving (November 28), Black Friday and Cyber Monday (December 2), the company announced on November 18. For brands, the selling event now starts six days before Thanksgiving and runs eleven days to Cyber Monday.

What happened

Amazon’s US announcement sets the calendar for Cyber Week 2019. It promises more Deals of the Day than before, a “Watch a Lightning Deal” alert in the Amazon app, and Prime Free One-Day Delivery on more than 10 million items, with Same-Day Delivery in 46 metro areas.

The US schedule matches what Amazon set out for the UK on November 5, when it announced an eight-day Black Friday sale from November 22 to November 29, with new Lightning Deals as often as every five minutes.

The season around it is short. Thanksgiving falls on November 28, so there are 22 days between Cyber Monday and Christmas, six fewer than in 2018, Adobe noted in its holiday forecast on October 21. Adobe expects about $29 billion of US online sales in Cyber Week, almost 20% of the November–December total, and $9.4 billion on Cyber Monday.

Why it matters for brands

The event is longer than the five days most plans are built around. A brand that budgets for Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday will meet Amazon’s deal traffic from November 22, with six days of competing deals before its own plan begins.

Daily budgets set for an ordinary week will run out early. With Deals of the Day changing daily and Lightning Deals cycling through the day, shoppers arrive at all hours, and sponsored ads that stop at mid-afternoon miss the evening.

One-day delivery shapes what sells late. With more than 10 million items eligible for free one-day delivery for Prime members, products in stock in Amazon’s network can sell closer to Christmas than seller-fulfilled products, which matters more in a season six days shorter.

What to do now

  1. Move the start of your Cyber Week budget and bid plan to November 22, and set daily budgets for each of the eleven days through December 2.
  2. Check that every product with a deal, and every product advertised against deal searches, has stock in Amazon’s network before November 22.
  3. Mark the 22 days from Cyber Monday to Christmas as a separate plan, with its own budget and a last-order date for each fulfillment method.

P0321.title: Cyber Week 2019 early read: Thanksgiving and Black Friday set online records but land just under Adobe’s forecast
P0321.alt: Blue, red and orange paper shopping bags lined up on a weathered wooden bench against a sunlit cream wall.
P0321.ttag: Cyber Week 2019 early read: Thanksgiving and Black Friday set online records but land just under Adobe’s forecast | Kwontified
P0321.desc: Preliminary figures from Adobe Analytics show US shoppers spent a record $4.2 billion online on Thanksgiving Day and $7.4 billion on Black Friday 2019,…
P0321.byline: By Kwontified. Published Dec 3, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0321.body:
Preliminary figures from Adobe Analytics show US shoppers spent a record $4.2 billion online on Thanksgiving Day and $7.4 billion on Black Friday 2019, both slightly below Adobe’s own forecasts, CNBC reported on November 29 and CNN reported on November 30. Cyber Monday ran on December 2; its result was not yet published when this item was written, so every number below is an early read.

What happened

Thanksgiving set a record and missed the forecast. Online spending reached $4.2 billion, up 14.5% from 2018 and the first year above $4 billion, against Adobe’s estimate of $4.4 billion, according to CNBC. Adobe tracks 80 of the top 100 US online retailers.

Black Friday did the same. Shoppers spent $7.4 billion online, with $2.9 billion of it on smartphones, the biggest mobile day on record, CNN reported. Adobe had forecast $7.5 billion for the day, Fox Business reported in October.

The rest of the week is still a projection. Adobe projected $9.4 billion for Cyber Monday and about $29 billion for the five days from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, according to CNN. In its October forecast, Adobe said the season had six fewer peak shopping days than 2018 and only 22 days between Cyber Monday and Christmas, a squeeze it estimated would cost almost $1 billion in potential revenue, Adobe’s forecast said.

Store pickup took a large share. About 40% of online shoppers so far had chosen buy online, pick up in store, CNBC reported.

Why it matters for brands

The headline records hide a small shortfall. Two days running, online sales landed a few percent under Adobe’s forecast, so a plan built on the forecast has a gap to explain before anyone reads the final week as a win.

Part of the week was sold before it started. Retailers opened offers early to make up for the short season, which Adobe expected in October, so some Cyber Week orders may have been pulled forward from mid-November rather than added.

Phones carry more of the sale. With $2.9 billion of Black Friday spending on smartphones, the mobile product page, with its first image and the price above the fold, is where much of the week was decided.

What to do now

  1. Hold the Cyber Week recap until Cyber Monday’s final figures and your own data through December 2 are in; label anything earlier as preliminary.
  2. Compare November 1 to December 2 as a whole against the same period in 2018, not Black Friday against Black Friday, so early deals are counted on both sides.
  3. Check stock on your top sellers now: with only 22 days between Cyber Monday and Christmas, a stockout in the next two weeks costs more than usual.

P0326.crumb: Amazon bars sellers from using FedEx…
P0326.title: Amazon bars sellers from using FedEx Ground for Prime orders through the holidays
P0326.alt: A shrink-wrapped pallet of cardboard boxes beside a yellow pallet jack against a gray wall.
P0326.ttag: Amazon bars sellers from using FedEx Ground for Prime orders through the holidays | Kwontified
P0326.desc: Amazon has barred third-party sellers from using FedEx Ground to deliver Prime orders through the holidays, saying FedEx’s delivery performance is…
P0326.byline: By Kwontified. Published Dec 17, 2019. 2-minute read.
P0326.body:
Amazon has barred third-party sellers from using FedEx Ground to deliver Prime orders through the holidays, saying FedEx’s delivery performance is slipping, Bloomberg reported on December 16, 2019. Sellers received the message on the night of December 15, according to merchant notifications Bloomberg reviewed. The Wall Street Journal first reported the change.

What happened

The ban covers FedEx Ground on Prime orders. Sellers who fulfill their own Prime orders can no longer hand them to FedEx’s ground network; they can still use FedEx Express, which costs more, or switch carriers such as UPS, according to Bloomberg. The restriction is described as temporary, with no end date given, the Associated Press reported.

FedEx played it down. The company said the overall impact on its business is “minuscule,” Bloomberg reported, and told the AP that the decision affects a very small number of shippers but limits the options for small businesses on some of the busiest shipping days of the year.

The two companies were already apart. FedEx ended its ground and air delivery work for Amazon earlier in 2019, though third-party sellers could still use FedEx, the AP said. Third-party sellers account for more than half of the items sold on Amazon.com.

Why it matters for brands

Prime is a delivery promise that Amazon enforces on the seller. A brand that ships its own Prime orders carries the badge only while its carrier meets Amazon’s timing, and Amazon has now shown it will remove a carrier from that promise mid-season, with about a week of shipping left before Christmas.

Costs move with the carrier. Switching from FedEx Ground to FedEx Express or another ground network the week before Christmas means new rates, new pickup schedules and labels printed through new accounts, all at peak volume.

The lesson reaches beyond FedEx. Amazon is now judging carriers, not only sellers, on seller-fulfilled Prime orders, so a brand’s choice of carrier is now part of its Prime eligibility, not only its shipping budget.

What to do now

  1. If you ship Prime orders yourself, check which carrier and service each warehouse uses today and move any FedEx Ground Prime volume to an allowed service before your next pickup.
  2. Reprice your last-week holiday shipping: compare the cost of Express or another carrier with the margin on each Prime order, and pause Prime on items where the faster service turns the order unprofitable.
  3. After the holidays, write a second carrier into your seller-fulfilled Prime plan so a single carrier’s status can no longer take the badge off your listings.
